query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled level of carbon doping into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will enhance the glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state compared to the same alloy without carbon.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) prepared under conditions that normally yield partial crystallinity or limited amorphous regions upon rapid cooling.
generation.intervention: Add a controlled, optimal concentration of carbon during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Under rapid solidification conditions (e.g., melt-spinning or accelerated cooling) where the amorphous phase is otherwise attainable; the carbon level must be low enough to avoid phase separation or the formation of carbides.
generation.structural_mediator: Carbon atoms that integrate into the matrix modify the local bonding environment, disrupt long-range atomic order, and increase the effective configurational entropy.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating carbon, the local atomic interactions are altered (through potential covalent bonding character and atomic size effects), which retards crystal nucleation and growth. This leads to a higher energy barrier for crystallization during cooling and improves the thermal stability of the already-formed amorphous phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloy is expected to display a larger amorphous phase fraction and an increase in the crystallization onset temperature (as measured by DSC) relative to an otherwise similar phosphorus-containing alloy without carbon doping.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy produced and rapidly cooled without any carbon doping.
generation.boundary: Enhancements are predicted only at an optimal carbon doping level; excessive carbon may lead to carbide formation or microstructural inhomogeneities, and under slower cooling rates the intervention may not yield noticeable benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal carbon concentration and the magnitude of the improvement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability remain to be quantified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples—one with the optimized level of carbon doping and one without doping. Process both sets under identical rapid cooling conditions (e.g., via melt-spinning). Characterize the samples using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the amorphous phase fraction, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure crystallization onset temperatures, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe microstructural differences.
measurements: Quantitative amorphous phase fraction via XRD intensity analysis
Crystallization onset temperature and peak exotherm from DSC
Microstructural features and phase homogeneity via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in the amorphous phase fraction and an elevation in crystallization onset temperature compared to the undoped samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are an innovative class of materials that have gained substantial interest in recent decades due to their unique structural and functional properties, which surpass those of conventional alloys in several applications [,]. Unlike traditional alloys, which are often based on one or two main elements, HEAs typically comprise five or more principal elements in near-equimolar ratios. This high configurational entropy stabilizes simple solid-solution phases, thereby enhancing the alloy’s thermal stability and resistance to wear, corrosion, and mechanical stress [,,]. While many studies have focused on traditional high-entropy alloys, there is a limited understanding of how phosphorus addition combined with varied cooling rates influences phase transformations and microstructural development in HEAs. This study aims to address this gap by systematically investigating the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy under different cooling conditions. The discovery of the equimolar CrMnFeCoNi alloy, also known as the Cantor alloy, has inspired extensive research on HEAs due to its exceptional combination of strength and ductility across a wide temperature range [,,,,]. reading.lever: Introduce a controlled level of carbon doping into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys to enhance both amorphization and thermal stability.
reading.why: Carbon doping has improved glass-forming ability and thermal stability in related Cantor compositions, suggesting a promising intervention for phosphorus-containing systems.
